title: Slot pools and leaky-basin admission — design notes
content:
Context and goal:

- Problem we continuously see: noisy tenants or sudden sequence-length spikes cause sustained high GPU latency variance. When this happens, global throughput suffers because greedy admission and undifferentiated queues let a few tenants monopolize queue slots and KV-cache pressure reduces effective batching.

- Goal: design an admission controller that (1) enforces per-tenant fairness / priority, (2) keeps tail latency within SLOs, (3) plays nicely with prefix/KV cache hotness, and (4) provides predictable failure modes so higher-level apps can implement graceful degradation.

Executive summary (one-liner):

- Introduce slot pools per-tenant with a leaky-basin overflow mechanism, combined with a timeout coordinator and cache-aware admission heuristic. Slot pools provide long-term steady fairness; leaky basin handles transient bursts; the timeout coordinator enforces soft and hard deadlines; and cache-aware heuristics prefer admitting requests that are likely to hit the KV/prefix cache.

Key concepts and definitions:

- slot: a short-lived reservation representing a request's right to enter the active serving set and consume GPU KV/batching resources for the next token window. Slots are released at token boundaries or upon request completion.

- slot pool: each tenant T has a configurable pool size S_T that represents its guaranteed concurrency. Pools are hierarchical (tenant -> team -> org) for enterprise rollups. Pools are adjustable by autoscale policies.

- leaky basin: an overflow buffer per-host (not per-tenant) that accepts bursts beyond pool guarantees but drains at a controlled rate (leak rate). The basin has leak priorities and a small fast-eviction path for extremely long requests.

- cache-affinity score: a heuristic computed per-request using prefix fingerprint, prompt length, and last-seen KV cache state. Higher score means higher expected KV hit and thus lower marginal GPU cost.

- soft timeout / hard timeout: soft timeout triggers polite cancellation (for streaming: send a partial chunk + EOF), hard timeout forcibly terminates and marks as shed.

Admission rules (high-level):

1) Steady-state: each tenant consumes up to its slot pool S_T. Requests beyond S_T are queued in a per-tenant pending queue up to Q_T. Queue ordering uses weighted priority (priority header > cache-affinity > arrival time).

2) Burst handling: if host-wide free slots exist and leaky basin capacity remains, requests above S_T may be admitted into basin slots. Basin drains at host-configured leak_rate L (tokens/sec) and uses a weighted fair share across tenants currently in the basin. Basin admission caps per-tenant to avoid single-tenant monopolization during bursts.

3) Emergency shedding: when overall host load or GPU memory pressure exceeds critical thresholds (configurable metrics), the controller applies shedding in stages: (i) reject new low-priority traffic (based on tenant SLAs), (ii) evict old basin entries (LRU by prefix-affinity penalty), (iii) kill long-running requests if beyond hard timeout.

4) Timeout coordination: every admitted request has (soft_timeout_ms, hard_timeout_ms). Soft timeout defaults are derived from model profile + kernel variance estimate. Soft timeouts prompt graceful stop and opportunistic cache retention decisions (e.g., keep KV for partial outputs). Hard timeouts are strict and enforced by the runtime kernel watchdog.

Cache-aware admission details:

- Motivation: KV cache hits dramatically reduce per-token compute and reduce tail latency. We should bias admission toward requests likely to reuse the cache.

- Mechanics:
  - compute cache-affinity score at enqueue time. Score components: prefix_hash_hit_rate_estimate (from sampling), prompt_similarity_to_hot_prefixes (cosine estimate from short embedding hist), expected continuation length (model/route hint).
  - if affinity > threshold_A and pool is exhausted, allow short-circuit admission into a transient fast-path slot (small token budget, e.g., 8 tokens) that is favored to complete quickly and release KV. This reduces chance of cache thrashing.

- Interaction with eviction: when memory pressure requires KV evictions, prefer evicting cold prefixes; keep hot prefixes reserved using a small reserved-KV quota per-tenant (configurable).

Kernel & model-profile integration:

- The scheduler consumes a per-model variance profile published by compilation: {p50, p95, p99 per sequence-length buckets, memory footprint, kernel_config_hash}. Use these to compute default soft_timeout margins and basin leak_rate tuning.

- Example default policy derivation: for model m with p95 latency 120ms at seq=512, set soft_timeout = p95 * 1.6, hard_timeout = p99 * 2.0 (config knobs). For quantized kernels with low variance, shrink margins.

Per-tenant config surface (suggested):

- guaranteed_slots (S_T) — integer
- max_pending_queue (Q_T) — integer
- burst_headroom (B_T) — tokens tenant can use in basin per minute
- reserved_kv_bytes — soft reservation for hot prefixes
- priority_tier — realtime | standard | background
- timeout_multiplier — overrides default soft/hard multiplier

Metrics to expose (minimal list):

- tenant.current_slots_used (gauge)
- tenant.pending_queue_depth (gauge)
- tenant.basin_entries (gauge)
- host.basin_fill_ratio (gauge)
- admission.decisions.{admitted,queued,basin,refused,evicted} (counters)
- request.latency.{p50,p95,p99} per-tenant-per-model
- kv.cache_hit_ratio (per-prefix and aggregated)
- kernel.variance_estimate (derived)

Open tradeoffs and questions (notes to self):

- Basin vs global overflow queue: we chose a host-level basin to allow immediate short-lived bursts across tenants; however this complicates debugging (spreading blame). Consider adding a debug-mode where basin is disabled and overflow becomes explicit queue entries.

- Leasing vs slots: Should slots be lease-based (time-expiring) or strictly returned at token boundary? Leases reduce the risk of hung requests permanently holding slots but complicate batching correctness. Proposal: primary lifecycle is returned-on-completion; fallback watchdog enforces lease timeouts slightly above hard_timeout.

- Autoscaling interactions: Dedicated nodes with autoscale mean slot guarantees can be expanded. How do we reconcile instantaneous basin admission with scale-up delays? Idea: if admission fails due to capacity and autoscale is possible, place request in a warm queue with exponential backoff and a marker that triggers immediate scale decisions.

- Fairness across teams/org rollups: top-level pools must be respected even if individual tenant pools are hungry. Implement hierarchical slot accounting to avoid noisy-team takeover.

Implementation plan (phases):

- Phase 0 (experiment): add telemetry for per-tenant KV hit rate, track top-n prefixes, and instrument current admission decisions. (owner: Connor, ETA: 2 weeks)

- Phase 1 (slot pools): implement per-tenant slot counters and pending queues; allow admin override of guaranteed_slots. Integrate with existing queuing code path. (owner: Aisha, ETA: 4 weeks)

- Phase 2 (leaky basin): implement host-level basin with leak controller, add basin admission path and plumbing to kernel watchdog for early evictions. (owner: Elena, ETA: 3 weeks)

- Phase 3 (cache affinity): wire prefix fingerprints + cheap embedding probe to compute cache-affinity; implement short-path fast-slot for high-affinity requests. (owner: Mateo, ETA: 4 weeks)

- Phase 4 (timeouts + policies): default timeout multipliers from model profiles, soft/hard enforcement, user-facing config. (owner: Aisha, ETA: 2 weeks)

- Phase 5 (ops and rollout): dashboards, SLO alerts for basin_fill_ratio and eviction rates, gradual rollouts by shard. (owner: eng-sre, ETA: 3 weeks)

Backward compatibility and migration notes:

- Default behavior remains unchanged until tenant-specific guaranteed_slots are set. Basin is off by default and enabled per-host via runtime flag for canary rollout.

- Need migration script to populate reserved_kv_bytes from historical KV footprints per-tenant.

Safety and observability checklist before rollout:

- [ ] Host-level knob to disable basin immediately
- [ ] Contention dashboard with tenant heatmap (slots used / guaranteed_slots)
- [ ] Alerts for sudden drop in kv.cache_hit_ratio and spike in host.basin_fill_ratio
- [ ] SLIs for soft-timeout-induced partial responses (make sure clients can handle)

Notes / loose thoughts (scratch):

- Could explore an optimistic admission mode where low-cost requests (predicted short tail) are admitted speculatively into pre-warmed micro-batches; if they mispredict, evict via basin.

- Consider a small per-host admission ML model (lightweight logistic) trained on prefix features to predict p(success < 200ms) — useful for offloading static heuristics later. Privacy note: only use aggregated prefix fingerprints, not raw data.

- We must be careful about fairness vs cost: enterprise customers pay for reserved capacity — billing events should reflect basin usage if persistent (flag as overage).

Action items:

- Aisha: draft API for per-tenant config page in console (fields listed above).
- Connor: add KV hit telemetry and top-prefix exporter.
- Elena: prototype basin leak controller as a standalone simulator (python).
- Mateo: prototype cheap prefix-affinity estimator (embedding-based sketch).

References and inspiration:

- leaky-bucket / token bucket QoS literature (adapt leaky-basin naming)
- cache-aware admission papers (e.g., web-cache locality scheduling)
- internal PRs: runtime/pull/2912 (batching improvements)
